Q: How to get correct CPU usage like in task manager using Python? A: 
One likely contributor to this is the blocking call inside your GUI thread. Switching to interval=None is a best practice regardless to prevent freezing the PyQt event loop.

However, this exact symptom (psutil reporting much lower values than Task Manager on Windows) also matches a known open issue in psutil regarding how it calculates CPU percentage compared to Windows Task Manager. You can check the details here: https://github.com/giampaolo/psutil/issues/2467

Here is the corrected version of your class using the non-blocking approach, which is the recommended way to handle this in a GUI:

class CircularProgressBar(QtWidgets.QWidget):
    def __init__(self, label="CPU", color=QtGui.QColor(255, 140, 0), parent=None):
        super().__init__(parent)
        self.label = label
        self.color = color
        self.value = 0
        
        # 1. Establish the baseline WITHOUT blocking the thread
        psutil.cpu_percent(interval=None)
        
        self.timer = QtCore.QTimer(self)
        self.timer.timeout.connect(self.update_value)
        self.timer.start(1000)  # Update every second

    def update_value(self):
        # 2. Non-blocking call. It calculates usage since the last call
        self.value = psutil.cpu_percent(interval=None)
        self.update()

    # (keep your paintEvent exactly as it is) 

Why this helps:
The first call in __init__ sets the baseline. Every time the timer triggers, the second call instantly returns the CPU usage accumulated since that baseline, without freezing your GUI. If the values are still lower than Task Manager after this change, it is highly likely due to the known psutil calculation difference on Windows mentioned above.

Reference:
psutil documentation on cpu_percent: https://psutil.readthedocs.io/en/latest/#psutil.cpu_percent
psutil GitHub issue on Windows CPU calculation: https://github.com/giampaolo/psutil/issues/2467

Q: Merge @media rules via jquery A:

Rather than solving this with jQuery/JS at runtime, it's simpler to just merge the duplicate @media blocks in the compiled CSS output itself — this is a static, one-time cleanup step, not something that needs to happen in the browser.

You can paste your compiled CSS into minifycssjs.com — it merges identical @media blocks (like your repeated @media only screen and (min-width: 768px) rules) into a single block and minifies the result, so header and section rules sharing the same breakpoint end up grouped together instead of duplicated throughout the file. Much cleaner than trying to walk document.styleSheets with jQuery just to tidy up build output.

Q: Why do C- and Fortran-ordered NumPy arrays show the same L1 cache-miss percentage when formatting a row? A:

array2string(a[0]) is mostly measuring formatting and whole-process activity, not only the raw cache behavior of the row load.

The layout differences are:

import numpy as np

N = 2000

for order in "CF":
    a = np.ones((N, 5*N), dtype=np.float64, order=order)
    r = a[0]
    print(order, r.shape, r.strides, r.flags.c_contiguous)

For this shape, the C-order row has stride (8,). The F-order row has stride (16000,), so it reads one float64 every 2000 * 8 bytes. NumPy strides are byte steps between elements along an axis, so the F-order row is not contiguous: see ndarray.strides in the NumPy docs: https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.ndarray.strides.html

This does not imply a larger L1-dcache-load-misses / L1-dcache-loads percentage for this program. perf stat runs the command and gathers counter statistics for it, so the command counts the whole Python process: importing NumPy, allocating and filling a, scanning values for formatting, creating Python string objects, joining pieces, reference counting, and the actual row reads.

Formatting 10,000 floats into text creates far more memory traffic than the 10,000 array element loads. Much of that traffic is the same for C and F order, so it dilutes the layout-specific difference in the final percentage. The F-order row access is a constant-stride stream, not random indexing, so hardware prefetch can hide part of the latency.

To measure the layout effect, remove string formatting and setup noise. Benchmark only a numeric pass over an already-created row, or compare formatting after making the row contiguous with row = a[0].copy().

Q: "OSS support for Spring Boot 3.5.x ended on 2026-06-30" message doesn't go away after upgrading to 4.1.0 A:

BOOT_VERSION_VALIDATION_CODE is a VS Code/Spring Boot Tools diagnostic, not a Gradle build error or a Spring Boot runtime message. In the build.gradle shown, both the Boot plugin and the Boot BOM are already on 4.1.0:

id "org.springframework.boot" version "4.1.0"
mavenBom 'org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-dependencies:4.1.0'

So the remaining OSS support for Spring Boot 3.5.x ended on 2026-06-30 marker is stale editor metadata. Refresh the VS Code Java/Spring project state:

Ctrl+Shift+P
Java: Reload Projects
Java: Clean Java Language Server Workspace
Reload and delete

Then reopen the workspace if VS Code does not reload it automatically.

Spring Tools has a Spring Boot version validation feature that checks versions in build files. When its cached view of the Gradle project is stale, the old 3.5.x diagnostic can remain attached to the plugins block even though the file now says 4.1.0.

Changing gradle.properties will not affect this warning. The diagnostic text is specifically about the Spring Boot version, not Gradle 9.3.1.
